# cadence - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cadence/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/cadence/index.html

## Expand description

An extensible Statsd client for Rust!

Cadence is a fast and flexible way to emit Statsd metrics from your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- [Support](https://docs.rs/cadence/)for emitting counters, timers, histograms, distributions, gauges, meters, and sets to Statsd over UDP (or optionally Unix sockets).
- Support for alternate backends via the `MetricSink`trait.
- Support for [Datadog](https://docs.datadoghq.com/developers/dogstatsd/)style metrics tags.
- [Macros](https://docs.rs/cadence-macros/)to simplify common calls to emit metrics
- A simple yet flexible API for sending metrics.

[§](https://docs.rs#install)Install

To make use of `cadence` in your project, add it as a dependency in your `Cargo.toml` file.

```
[dependencies]
cadence = "x.y.z"
```
That’s all you need!

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Some examples of how to use Cadence are shown below. The examples start simple and work up to how you should be using Cadence in a production application.

[§](https://docs.rs#simple-use)Simple Use

Simple usage of Cadence is shown below. In this example, we just import the client, create an instance that will write to some imaginary metrics server, and send a few metrics.

```
use std::net::UdpSocket;
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, UdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
// Create client that will write to the given host over UDP.
//
// Note that you'll probably want to actually handle any errors creating
// the client when you use it for real in your application. We're just
// using .unwrap() here since this is an example!
let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
let sink = UdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.metrics", sink);
// Emit metrics!
client.count("some.counter", 1);
client.time("some.methodCall", 42);
client.gauge("some.thing", 7);
client.meter("some.value", 5);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#buffered-udp-sink)Buffered UDP Sink

While sending a metric over UDP is very fast, the overhead of frequent network calls can start to add up. This is especially true if you are writing a high performance application that emits a lot of metrics.

To make sure that metrics aren’t interfering with the performance of
your application, you may want to use a `MetricSink` implementation that
buffers multiple metrics before sending them in a single network
operation. For this, there’s `BufferedUdpMetricSink`. An example of
using this sink is given below.

```
use std::net::UdpSocket;
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, BufferedUdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
socket.set_nonblocking(true).unwrap();
let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
let sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", sink);
client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
client.time("my.service.call", 214);
```
As you can see, using this buffered UDP sink is no more complicated than using the regular, non-buffered, UDP sink.

The only downside to this sink is that metrics aren’t written to the
Statsd server until the buffer is full. If you have a busy application
that is constantly emitting metrics, this shouldn’t be a problem.
However, if your application only occasionally emits metrics, this sink
might result in the metrics being delayed for a little while until the
buffer fills. In this case, it may make sense to use the `UdpMetricSink`
since it does not do any buffering.

[§](https://docs.rs#re-resolving-udp-sinks)Re-resolving UDP Sinks

When using UDP sinks by default, the address of the server you are sending metrics to is resolved a single time when the UDP sink is created. If you anticipate the IP address of the server you are sending metrics to will change, you can configure UDP sinks to periodically re-resolve the IP address of the metrics server. This can be done using their respective builders. You may also supply a function that is called when the re-resolution of the metrics server IP address fails.

```
use std::net::UdpSocket;
use std::time::Duration;
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, BufferedUdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
let sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::builder()
    .with_capacity(1024)
    .with_resolver_period(Duration::from_secs(5))
    .with_resolver_error_handler(|e| {
        eprintln!("error: failed to resolve host: {}", e);
    })
    .build(host, socket)
    .unwrap();
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", sink);
client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
client.time("my.service.call", 214);
```
If enabled, periodic address resolution is done in a separate thread created by the sink when the sink is created. The thread is stopped when the sink is dropped.

[§](https://docs.rs#queuing-asynchronous-metric-sink)Queuing Asynchronous Metric Sink

To make sure emitting metrics doesn’t interfere with the performance of your application (even though emitting metrics is generally quite fast), it’s probably a good idea to make sure metrics are emitted in in a different thread than your application thread.

To allow you to do this, there is `QueuingMetricSink`. This sink allows
you to wrap any other metric sink and send metrics to it via a queue,
as it emits metrics in another thread, asynchronously from the flow of
your application.

The requirements for the wrapped metric sink are that it is thread
safe, meaning that it implements the `Send` and `Sync` traits. If
you’re using the `QueuingMetricSink` with another sink from Cadence,
you don’t need to worry: they are all thread safe.

An example of using the `QueuingMetricSink` to wrap a buffered UDP
metric sink is given below. This is the preferred way to use Cadence
in production.

```
use std::net::UdpSocket;
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, QueuingMetricSink, BufferedUdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
socket.set_nonblocking(true).unwrap();
let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
let udp_sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
let queuing_sink = QueuingMetricSink::from(udp_sink);
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", queuing_sink);
client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
client.time("my.service.call", 214);
```
In the example above, we use the default constructor for the queuing
sink which creates an **unbounded** queue, with no maximum size, to connect
the main thread where the client sends metrics to the background thread
in which the wrapped sink is running. If instead, you want to create a
**bounded** queue with a maximum size, you can use the `with_capacity`
constructor. An example of this is given below.

```
use std::net::UdpSocket;
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, QueuingMetricSink, BufferedUdpMetricSink,
              DEFAULT_PORT};
// Queue with a maximum capacity of 128K elements
const QUEUE_SIZE: usize = 128 * 1024;
let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
socket.set_nonblocking(true).unwrap();
let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
let udp_sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
let queuing_sink = QueuingMetricSink::with_capacity(udp_sink, QUEUE_SIZE);
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", queuing_sink);
client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
client.time("my.service.call", 214);
```
Using a `QueuingMetricSink` with a capacity set means that when the queue
is full, attempts to emit metrics via the `StatsdClient` will fail. While
this is bad, the alternative (if you instead used an unbounded queue) is
for unsent metrics to slowly use up more and more memory until your
application exhausts all memory.

Using an **unbounded** queue means that the sending of metrics can absorb
slowdowns of sending metrics until your application runs out of memory.
Using a **bounded** queue puts a cap on the amount of memory that sending
metrics will use in your application. This is a tradeoff that users of
Cadence must decide for themselves.

It is also possible to supply an error handler for a `QueuingMetricSink` to
be called whenever the wrapped sink cannot send metrics for whatever reason.

```
use std::net::UdpSocket;
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, QueuingMetricSink, BufferedUdpMetricSink,
              DEFAULT_PORT};
// Queue with a maximum capacity of 128K elements
const QUEUE_SIZE: usize = 128 * 1024;
let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
socket.set_nonblocking(true).unwrap();
let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
let udp_sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
let queuing_sink = QueuingMetricSink::builder()
    .with_capacity(QUEUE_SIZE)
    .with_error_handler(|e| {
        eprintln!("Error while sending metrics: {:?}", e);
    })
    .build(udp_sink);
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", queuing_sink);
client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
client.time("my.service.call", 214);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-tags)Use With Tags

Adding tags to metrics is accomplished via the use of each of the `_with_tags`
methods that are part of the Cadence `StatsdClient` struct. An example of using
these methods is given below. Note that tags are an extension to the Statsd
protocol and so may not be supported by all servers.

See the [Datadog docs](https://docs.datadoghq.com/developers/dogstatsd/) for
more information.

```
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{Metric, StatsdClient, NopMetricSink};
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", NopMetricSink);
let res = client.count_with_tags("my.counter", 29)
    .with_tag("host", "web03.example.com")
    .with_tag_value("beta-test")
    .try_send();
assert_eq!(
    concat!(
        "my.prefix.my.counter:29|c|#",
        "host:web03.example.com,",
        "beta-test"
    ),
    res.unwrap().as_metric_str()
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#default-tags)Default Tags

Default tags can be added to a `StatsdClient` when constructed using the builder.
Default tags are added to every metric emitted by the `StatsdClient` without any
extra work after building the client. Note that tags are an extension to the Statsd
protocol and so may not be supported by all servers.

See the [Datadog docs](https://docs.datadoghq.com/developers/dogstatsd/) for
more information.

```
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{Metric, StatsdClient, NopMetricSink};
let client = StatsdClient::builder("my.prefix", NopMetricSink)
    .with_tag("env", "prod")
    .with_tag("app", "auth")
    .build();
let res = client.count_with_tags("my.counter", 29)
    .with_tag("host", "web03.example.com")
    .with_tag_value("beta-test")
    .try_send();
assert_eq!(
    concat!(
        "my.prefix.my.counter:29|c|#",
        "env:prod,",
        "app:auth,",
        "host:web03.example.com,",
        "beta-test"
    ),
    res.unwrap().as_metric_str()
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#value-packing)Value Packing

Value packing allows multiple values to be sent as a single metric for histograms,
distributions, and timer types. The Cadence client accepts `Vec<T>` for histogram,
distribution, and timer methods and will format multiple values as described below.
Note that this feature is a Datadog extension and so may not be supported by your
server. It is supported by versions `>=v6.25.0 && <v7.0.0` or `>=v7.25.0` of the
Datadog agent.

Packed metrics have the following format:

`<METRIC_NAME>:<VALUE1>:<VALUE2>:<VALUE3>|<TYPE>|#<TAG_KEY_1>:<TAG_VALUE_1>,<TAG_2>``See the [Datadog Docs](https://docs.datadoghq.com/developers/dogstatsd/datagram_shell/?tab=metrics#dogstatsd-protocol-v11)
for more information.

```
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{Metric, StatsdClient, NopMetricSink};
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", NopMetricSink);
let res = client.distribution_with_tags("my.distribution", vec![29, 30, 31, 32])
    .with_tag("host", "web03.example.com")
    .with_tag_value("beta-test")
    .try_send();
assert_eq!(
    concat!(
        "my.prefix.my.distribution:29:30:31:32|d|#",
        "host:web03.example.com,",
        "beta-test"
    ),
    res.unwrap().as_metric_str()
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implemented-traits)Implemented Traits

Each of the methods that the Cadence `StatsdClient` struct uses to send
metrics are implemented as a trait. There is also a trait that combines
all of these other traits. If we want, we can just use one of the trait
types to refer to the client instance. This might be useful to you if
you’d like to swap out the actual Cadence client with a dummy version
when you are unit testing your code or want to abstract away all the
implementation details of the client being used behind a trait and
pointer.

Each of these traits are exported in the prelude module. They are also available in the main module but aren’t typically used like that.

```
use std::net::UdpSocket;
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, UdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
pub struct User {
    id: u64,
    username: String,
    email: String
}
// Here's a simple DAO (Data Access Object) that doesn't do anything but
// uses a metric client to keep track of the number of times the
// 'getUserById' method gets called.
pub struct MyUserDao {
    metrics: Box<dyn MetricClient>
}
impl MyUserDao {
    // Create a new instance that will use the StatsdClient
    pub fn new<T: MetricClient + 'static>(metrics: T) -> MyUserDao {
        MyUserDao { metrics: Box::new(metrics) }
    }
    /// Get a new user by their ID
    pub fn get_user_by_id(&self, id: u64) -> Option<User> {
        self.metrics.count("getUserById", 1);
        None
    }
}
// Create a new Statsd client that writes to "metrics.example.com"
let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
let sink = UdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
let metrics = StatsdClient::from_sink("counter.example", sink);
// Create a new instance of the DAO that will use the client
let dao = MyUserDao::new(metrics);
// Try to lookup a user by ID!
match dao.get_user_by_id(123) {
    Some(u) => println!("Found a user!"),
    None => println!("No user!")
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#quiet-metric-sending-and-error-handling)Quiet Metric Sending and Error Handling

When sending metrics sometimes you don’t really care about the `Result` of
trying to send it or maybe you just don’t want to deal with it inline with
the rest of your code. In order to handle this, Cadence allows you to set a
default error handler. This handler is invoked when there are errors sending
metrics so that the calling code doesn’t have to deal with them.

An example of configuring an error handler and an example of when it might be invoked is given below.

```
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{MetricError, StatsdClient, NopMetricSink};
fn my_error_handler(err: MetricError) {
    println!("Metric error! {}", err);
}
let client = StatsdClient::builder("prefix", NopMetricSink)
    .with_error_handler(my_error_handler)
    .build();
// When sending metrics via the `MetricBuilder` used for assembling tags,
// callers may opt into sending metrics quietly via the `.send()` method
// as opposed to the `.try_send()` method
client.count_with_tags("some.counter", 42)
    .with_tag("region", "us-east-2")
    .send();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-metric-sinks)Custom Metric Sinks

The Cadence `StatsdClient` uses implementations of the `MetricSink`
trait to send metrics to a metric server. Most users of the Cadence
library probably want to use the `QueuingMetricSink` wrapping an instance
of the `BufferedMetricSink`.

However, maybe you want to do something not covered by an existing sink. An example of creating a custom sink is below.

```
use std::io;
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, MetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
pub struct MyMetricSink;
impl MetricSink for MyMetricSink {
    fn emit(&self, metric: &str) -> io::Result<usize> {
        // Your custom metric sink implementation goes here!
        Ok(0)
    }
}
let sink = MyMetricSink;
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", sink);
client.count("my.counter.thing", 42);
client.time("my.method.time", 25);
client.count("some.other.counter", 1);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-udp-socket)Custom UDP Socket

Most users of the Cadence `StatsdClient` will be using it to send metrics
over a UDP socket. If you need to customize the socket, for example you
want to use the socket in blocking mode but set a write timeout, you can
do that as demonstrated below.

```
use std::net::UdpSocket;
use std::time::Duration;
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, UdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
socket.set_write_timeout(Some(Duration::from_millis(1))).unwrap();
let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
let sink = UdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", sink);
client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
client.time("my.service.call", 214);
client.count("some.event", 33);
client.set("users.uniques", 42);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#unix-sockets)Unix Sockets

Cadence also supports using Unix datagram sockets with the `UnixMetricSink`  or
`BufferedUnixMetricSink`. Unix sockets can be used for sending metrics to a server
or agent running on the same machine (physical machine, VM, containers in a pod)
as your application. Unix sockets are somewhat similar to UDP sockets with a few
important differences:

- Sending metrics on a socket that doesn’t exist or is not being listened to will result in an error.
- Metrics sent on a connected socket are guaranteed to be delievered (i.e. they are reliable as opposed to UDP sockets). However, it’s still possible that the metrics won’t be read by the server due to a variety of environment and server specific reasons.

An example of using the sinks is given below.

```
use std::os::unix::net::UnixDatagram;
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, BufferedUnixMetricSink};
let socket = UnixDatagram::unbound().unwrap();
socket.set_nonblocking(true).unwrap();
let sink = BufferedUnixMetricSink::from("/run/statsd.sock", socket);
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", sink);
client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
client.time("my.service.call", 214);
client.count("some.event", 33);
client.set("users.uniques", 42);
```
NOTE: This feature is only available on Unix platforms (Linux, BSD, MacOS).

# cadence/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)// Cadence - An extensible Statsd client for Rust!
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//
[3](https://docs.rs#3)// Copyright 2015-2021 Nick Pillitteri
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//
[5](https://docs.rs#5)// Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 <LICENSE-APACHE or
[6](https://docs.rs#6)// http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0> or the MIT license
[7](https://docs.rs#7)// <LICENSE-MIT or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT>, at your
[8](https://docs.rs#8)// option. This file may not be copied, modified, or distributed
[9](https://docs.rs#9)// except according to those terms.
[10](https://docs.rs#10)
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! An extensible Statsd client for Rust!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! Cadence is a fast and flexible way to emit Statsd metrics from your application.
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! ## Features
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! * [Support](https://docs.rs/cadence/) for emitting counters, timers, histograms, distributions,
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!   gauges, meters, and sets to Statsd over UDP (or optionally Unix sockets).
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! * Support for alternate backends via the `MetricSink` trait.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! * Support for [Datadog](https://docs.datadoghq.com/developers/dogstatsd/) style metrics tags.
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! * [Macros](https://docs.rs/cadence-macros/) to simplify common calls to emit metrics
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! * A simple yet flexible API for sending metrics.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! ## Install
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! To make use of `cadence` in your project, add it as a dependency in your `Cargo.toml` file.
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! ```toml
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! [dependencies]
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! cadence = "x.y.z"
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! ```
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! That's all you need!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! ## Usage
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! Some examples of how to use Cadence are shown below. The examples start
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! simple and work up to how you should be using Cadence in a production
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! application.
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! ### Simple Use
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! Simple usage of Cadence is shown below. In this example, we just import
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! the client, create an instance that will write to some imaginary metrics
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! server, and send a few metrics.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! ```rust,no_run
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! use std::net::UdpSocket;
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! use cadence::{StatsdClient, UdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! // Create client that will write to the given host over UDP.
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! //
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! // Note that you'll probably want to actually handle any errors creating
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! // the client when you use it for real in your application. We're just
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! // using .unwrap() here since this is an example!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! let sink = UdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.metrics", sink);
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! // Emit metrics!
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! client.count("some.counter", 1);
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! client.time("some.methodCall", 42);
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! client.gauge("some.thing", 7);
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! client.meter("some.value", 5);
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! ```
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! ### Buffered UDP Sink
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! While sending a metric over UDP is very fast, the overhead of frequent
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! network calls can start to add up. This is especially true if you are
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! writing a high performance application that emits a lot of metrics.
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! To make sure that metrics aren't interfering with the performance of
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! your application, you may want to use a `MetricSink` implementation that
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! buffers multiple metrics before sending them in a single network
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! operation. For this, there's `BufferedUdpMetricSink`. An example of
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! using this sink is given below.
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! ```rust,no_run
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! use std::net::UdpSocket;
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! use cadence::{StatsdClient, BufferedUdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! socket.set_nonblocking(true).unwrap();
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! let sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", sink);
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! client.time("my.service.call", 214);
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! ```
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! As you can see, using this buffered UDP sink is no more complicated
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! than using the regular, non-buffered, UDP sink.
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! The only downside to this sink is that metrics aren't written to the
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! Statsd server until the buffer is full. If you have a busy application
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! that is constantly emitting metrics, this shouldn't be a problem.
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! However, if your application only occasionally emits metrics, this sink
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! might result in the metrics being delayed for a little while until the
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! buffer fills. In this case, it may make sense to use the `UdpMetricSink`
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! since it does not do any buffering.
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! ### Re-resolving UDP Sinks
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! When using UDP sinks by default, the address of the server you are
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! sending metrics to is resolved a single time when the UDP sink is
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! created. If you anticipate the IP address of the server you are sending
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! metrics to will change, you can configure UDP sinks to periodically
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! re-resolve the IP address of the metrics server. This can be done using
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! their respective builders. You may also supply a function that is
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! called when the re-resolution of the metrics server IP address fails.
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! ```rust,no_run
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! use std::net::UdpSocket;
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! use std::time::Duration;
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! use cadence::{StatsdClient, BufferedUdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! let sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::builder()
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!     .with_capacity(1024)
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!     .with_resolver_period(Duration::from_secs(5))
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!     .with_resolver_error_handler(|e| {
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!         eprintln!("error: failed to resolve host: {}", e);
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!     })
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!     .build(host, socket)
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!     .unwrap();
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", sink);
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! client.time("my.service.call", 214);
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! ```
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! If enabled, periodic address resolution is done in a separate thread
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! created by the sink when the sink is created. The thread is stopped
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! when the sink is dropped.
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! ### Queuing Asynchronous Metric Sink
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! To make sure emitting metrics doesn't interfere with the performance
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! of your application (even though emitting metrics is generally quite
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! fast), it's probably a good idea to make sure metrics are emitted in
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! in a different thread than your application thread.
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! To allow you to do this, there is `QueuingMetricSink`. This sink allows
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! you to wrap any other metric sink and send metrics to it via a queue,
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! as it emits metrics in another thread, asynchronously from the flow of
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! your application.
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! The requirements for the wrapped metric sink are that it is thread
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! safe, meaning that it implements the `Send` and `Sync` traits. If
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! you're using the `QueuingMetricSink` with another sink from Cadence,
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! you don't need to worry: they are all thread safe.
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! An example of using the `QueuingMetricSink` to wrap a buffered UDP
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! metric sink is given below. This is the preferred way to use Cadence
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! in production.
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! ```rust,no_run
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! use std::net::UdpSocket;
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! use cadence::{StatsdClient, QueuingMetricSink, BufferedUdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//!
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! socket.set_nonblocking(true).unwrap();
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//!
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! let udp_sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! let queuing_sink = QueuingMetricSink::from(udp_sink);
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", queuing_sink);
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! client.time("my.service.call", 214);
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! ```
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//!
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! In the example above, we use the default constructor for the queuing
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! sink which creates an **unbounded** queue, with no maximum size, to connect
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! the main thread where the client sends metrics to the background thread
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! in which the wrapped sink is running. If instead, you want to create a
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! **bounded** queue with a maximum size, you can use the `with_capacity`
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! constructor. An example of this is given below.
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! ```rust,no_run
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! use std::net::UdpSocket;
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! use cadence::{StatsdClient, QueuingMetricSink, BufferedUdpMetricSink,
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//!               DEFAULT_PORT};
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//!
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! // Queue with a maximum capacity of 128K elements
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! const QUEUE_SIZE: usize = 128 * 1024;
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! socket.set_nonblocking(true).unwrap();
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! let udp_sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! let queuing_sink = QueuingMetricSink::with_capacity(udp_sink, QUEUE_SIZE);
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", queuing_sink);
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//!
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! client.time("my.service.call", 214);
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! ```
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//!
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! Using a `QueuingMetricSink` with a capacity set means that when the queue
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! is full, attempts to emit metrics via the `StatsdClient` will fail. While
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! this is bad, the alternative (if you instead used an unbounded queue) is
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! for unsent metrics to slowly use up more and more memory until your
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! application exhausts all memory.
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//!
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! Using an **unbounded** queue means that the sending of metrics can absorb
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! slowdowns of sending metrics until your application runs out of memory.
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! Using a **bounded** queue puts a cap on the amount of memory that sending
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! metrics will use in your application. This is a tradeoff that users of
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! Cadence must decide for themselves.
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//!
[224](https://docs.rs#224)
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! It is also possible to supply an error handler for a `QueuingMetricSink` to
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! be called whenever the wrapped sink cannot send metrics for whatever reason.
[227](https://docs.rs#227)
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! ```rust,no_run
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! use std::net::UdpSocket;
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! use cadence::{StatsdClient, QueuingMetricSink, BufferedUdpMetricSink,
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//!               DEFAULT_PORT};
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! // Queue with a maximum capacity of 128K elements
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//! const QUEUE_SIZE: usize = 128 * 1024;
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//!
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! socket.set_nonblocking(true).unwrap();
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//! let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! let udp_sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! let queuing_sink = QueuingMetricSink::builder()
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//!     .with_capacity(QUEUE_SIZE)
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!     .with_error_handler(|e| {
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//!         eprintln!("Error while sending metrics: {:?}", e);
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//!     })
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//!     .build(udp_sink);
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", queuing_sink);
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! client.time("my.service.call", 214);
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! ```
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! ### Use With Tags
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//!
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//! Adding tags to metrics is accomplished via the use of each of the `_with_tags`
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! methods that are part of the Cadence `StatsdClient` struct. An example of using
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//! these methods is given below. Note that tags are an extension to the Statsd
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! protocol and so may not be supported by all servers.
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//!
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! See the [Datadog docs](https://docs.datadoghq.com/developers/dogstatsd/) for
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//! more information.
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//! ```rust,no_run
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//! use cadence::{Metric, StatsdClient, NopMetricSink};
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//!
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//! let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", NopMetricSink);
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//!
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//! let res = client.count_with_tags("my.counter", 29)
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//!     .with_tag("host", "web03.example.com")
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//!     .with_tag_value("beta-test")
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//!     .try_send();
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//!
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! assert_eq!(
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//!     concat!(
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//!         "my.prefix.my.counter:29|c|#",
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//!         "host:web03.example.com,",
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//!         "beta-test"
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//!     ),
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//!     res.unwrap().as_metric_str()
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! );
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! ```
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//!
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//! ### Default Tags
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//!
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//! Default tags can be added to a `StatsdClient` when constructed using the builder.
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! Default tags are added to every metric emitted by the `StatsdClient` without any
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//! extra work after building the client. Note that tags are an extension to the Statsd
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! protocol and so may not be supported by all servers.
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//!
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//! See the [Datadog docs](https://docs.datadoghq.com/developers/dogstatsd/) for
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//! more information.
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//!
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//! ```rust,no_run
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//! use cadence::{Metric, StatsdClient, NopMetricSink};
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//!
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//! let client = StatsdClient::builder("my.prefix", NopMetricSink)
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//!     .with_tag("env", "prod")
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//!     .with_tag("app", "auth")
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//!     .build();
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//!
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//! let res = client.count_with_tags("my.counter", 29)
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//!     .with_tag("host", "web03.example.com")
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//!     .with_tag_value("beta-test")
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//!     .try_send();
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//!
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//! assert_eq!(
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//!     concat!(
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//!         "my.prefix.my.counter:29|c|#",
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//!         "env:prod,",
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//!         "app:auth,",
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//!         "host:web03.example.com,",
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//!         "beta-test"
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//!     ),
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//!     res.unwrap().as_metric_str()
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//! );
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//! ```
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//!
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//! ### Value Packing
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//!
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//! Value packing allows multiple values to be sent as a single metric for histograms,
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//! distributions, and timer types. The Cadence client accepts `Vec<T>` for histogram,
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//! distribution, and timer methods and will format multiple values as described below.
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//! Note that this feature is a Datadog extension and so may not be supported by your
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//! server. It is supported by versions `>=v6.25.0 && <v7.0.0` or `>=v7.25.0` of the
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//! Datadog agent.
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//! Packed metrics have the following format:
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//! ```text
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//! <METRIC_NAME>:<VALUE1>:<VALUE2>:<VALUE3>|<TYPE>|#<TAG_KEY_1>:<TAG_VALUE_1>,<TAG_2>`
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//! ```
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//!
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//! See the [Datadog Docs](https://docs.datadoghq.com/developers/dogstatsd/datagram_shell/?tab=metrics#dogstatsd-protocol-v11)
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//! for more information.
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//!
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//! ```rust,no_run
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//! use cadence::{Metric, StatsdClient, NopMetricSink};
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//!
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//! let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", NopMetricSink);
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//!
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//! let res = client.distribution_with_tags("my.distribution", vec![29, 30, 31, 32])
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//!     .with_tag("host", "web03.example.com")
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//!     .with_tag_value("beta-test")
[347](https://docs.rs#347)//!     .try_send();
[348](https://docs.rs#348)//!
[349](https://docs.rs#349)//! assert_eq!(
[350](https://docs.rs#350)//!     concat!(
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//!         "my.prefix.my.distribution:29:30:31:32|d|#",
[352](https://docs.rs#352)//!         "host:web03.example.com,",
[353](https://docs.rs#353)//!         "beta-test"
[354](https://docs.rs#354)//!     ),
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//!     res.unwrap().as_metric_str()
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//! );
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//! ```
[358](https://docs.rs#358)//!
[359](https://docs.rs#359)//! ### Implemented Traits
[360](https://docs.rs#360)//!
[361](https://docs.rs#361)//! Each of the methods that the Cadence `StatsdClient` struct uses to send
[362](https://docs.rs#362)//! metrics are implemented as a trait. There is also a trait that combines
[363](https://docs.rs#363)//! all of these other traits. If we want, we can just use one of the trait
[364](https://docs.rs#364)//! types to refer to the client instance. This might be useful to you if
[365](https://docs.rs#365)//! you'd like to swap out the actual Cadence client with a dummy version
[366](https://docs.rs#366)//! when you are unit testing your code or want to abstract away all the
[367](https://docs.rs#367)//! implementation details of the client being used behind a trait and
[368](https://docs.rs#368)//! pointer.
[369](https://docs.rs#369)//!
[370](https://docs.rs#370)//! Each of these traits are exported in the prelude module. They are also
[371](https://docs.rs#371)//! available in the main module but aren't typically used like that.
[372](https://docs.rs#372)//!
[373](https://docs.rs#373)//! ```rust,no_run
[374](https://docs.rs#374)//! use std::net::UdpSocket;
[375](https://docs.rs#375)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[376](https://docs.rs#376)//! use cadence::{StatsdClient, UdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
[377](https://docs.rs#377)//!
[378](https://docs.rs#378)//! pub struct User {
[379](https://docs.rs#379)//!     id: u64,
[380](https://docs.rs#380)//!     username: String,
[381](https://docs.rs#381)//!     email: String
[382](https://docs.rs#382)//! }
[383](https://docs.rs#383)//!
[384](https://docs.rs#384)//!
[385](https://docs.rs#385)//! // Here's a simple DAO (Data Access Object) that doesn't do anything but
[386](https://docs.rs#386)//! // uses a metric client to keep track of the number of times the
[387](https://docs.rs#387)//! // 'getUserById' method gets called.
[388](https://docs.rs#388)//! pub struct MyUserDao {
[389](https://docs.rs#389)//!     metrics: Box<dyn MetricClient>
[390](https://docs.rs#390)//! }
[391](https://docs.rs#391)//!
[392](https://docs.rs#392)//!
[393](https://docs.rs#393)//! impl MyUserDao {
[394](https://docs.rs#394)//!     // Create a new instance that will use the StatsdClient
[395](https://docs.rs#395)//!     pub fn new<T: MetricClient + 'static>(metrics: T) -> MyUserDao {
[396](https://docs.rs#396)//!         MyUserDao { metrics: Box::new(metrics) }
[397](https://docs.rs#397)//!     }
[398](https://docs.rs#398)//!
[399](https://docs.rs#399)//!     /// Get a new user by their ID
[400](https://docs.rs#400)//!     pub fn get_user_by_id(&self, id: u64) -> Option<User> {
[401](https://docs.rs#401)//!         self.metrics.count("getUserById", 1);
[402](https://docs.rs#402)//!         None
[403](https://docs.rs#403)//!     }
[404](https://docs.rs#404)//! }
[405](https://docs.rs#405)//!
[406](https://docs.rs#406)//!
[407](https://docs.rs#407)//! // Create a new Statsd client that writes to "metrics.example.com"
[408](https://docs.rs#408)//! let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
[409](https://docs.rs#409)//! let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
[410](https://docs.rs#410)//! let sink = UdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
[411](https://docs.rs#411)//! let metrics = StatsdClient::from_sink("counter.example", sink);
[412](https://docs.rs#412)//!
[413](https://docs.rs#413)//! // Create a new instance of the DAO that will use the client
[414](https://docs.rs#414)//! let dao = MyUserDao::new(metrics);
[415](https://docs.rs#415)//!
[416](https://docs.rs#416)//! // Try to lookup a user by ID!
[417](https://docs.rs#417)//! match dao.get_user_by_id(123) {
[418](https://docs.rs#418)//!     Some(u) => println!("Found a user!"),
[419](https://docs.rs#419)//!     None => println!("No user!")
[420](https://docs.rs#420)//! };
[421](https://docs.rs#421)//! ```

[423](https://docs.rs#423)//! ### Quiet Metric Sending and Error Handling
[424](https://docs.rs#424)//!
[425](https://docs.rs#425)//! When sending metrics sometimes you don't really care about the `Result` of
[426](https://docs.rs#426)//! trying to send it or maybe you just don't want to deal with it inline with
[427](https://docs.rs#427)//! the rest of your code. In order to handle this, Cadence allows you to set a
[428](https://docs.rs#428)//! default error handler. This handler is invoked when there are errors sending
[429](https://docs.rs#429)//! metrics so that the calling code doesn't have to deal with them.
[430](https://docs.rs#430)//!
[431](https://docs.rs#431)//! An example of configuring an error handler and an example of when it might
[432](https://docs.rs#432)//! be invoked is given below.
[433](https://docs.rs#433)//!
[434](https://docs.rs#434)//! ```rust,no_run
[435](https://docs.rs#435)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[436](https://docs.rs#436)//! use cadence::{MetricError, StatsdClient, NopMetricSink};
[437](https://docs.rs#437)//!
[438](https://docs.rs#438)//! fn my_error_handler(err: MetricError) {
[439](https://docs.rs#439)//!     println!("Metric error! {}", err);
[440](https://docs.rs#440)//! }
[441](https://docs.rs#441)//!
[442](https://docs.rs#442)//! let client = StatsdClient::builder("prefix", NopMetricSink)
[443](https://docs.rs#443)//!     .with_error_handler(my_error_handler)
[444](https://docs.rs#444)//!     .build();
[445](https://docs.rs#445)//!
[446](https://docs.rs#446)//! // When sending metrics via the `MetricBuilder` used for assembling tags,
[447](https://docs.rs#447)//! // callers may opt into sending metrics quietly via the `.send()` method
[448](https://docs.rs#448)//! // as opposed to the `.try_send()` method
[449](https://docs.rs#449)//! client.count_with_tags("some.counter", 42)
[450](https://docs.rs#450)//!     .with_tag("region", "us-east-2")
[451](https://docs.rs#451)//!     .send();
[452](https://docs.rs#452)//! ```
[453](https://docs.rs#453)//!
[454](https://docs.rs#454)//! ### Custom Metric Sinks
[455](https://docs.rs#455)//!
[456](https://docs.rs#456)//! The Cadence `StatsdClient` uses implementations of the `MetricSink`
[457](https://docs.rs#457)//! trait to send metrics to a metric server. Most users of the Cadence
[458](https://docs.rs#458)//! library probably want to use the `QueuingMetricSink` wrapping an instance
[459](https://docs.rs#459)//! of the `BufferedMetricSink`.
[460](https://docs.rs#460)//!
[461](https://docs.rs#461)//! However, maybe you want to do something not covered by an existing sink.
[462](https://docs.rs#462)//! An example of creating a custom sink is below.
[463](https://docs.rs#463)//!
[464](https://docs.rs#464)//! ```rust,no_run
[465](https://docs.rs#465)//! use std::io;
[466](https://docs.rs#466)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[467](https://docs.rs#467)//! use cadence::{StatsdClient, MetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
[468](https://docs.rs#468)//!
[469](https://docs.rs#469)//! pub struct MyMetricSink;
[470](https://docs.rs#470)//!
[471](https://docs.rs#471)//!
[472](https://docs.rs#472)//! impl MetricSink for MyMetricSink {
[473](https://docs.rs#473)//!     fn emit(&self, metric: &str) -> io::Result<usize> {
[474](https://docs.rs#474)//!         // Your custom metric sink implementation goes here!
[475](https://docs.rs#475)//!         Ok(0)
[476](https://docs.rs#476)//!     }
[477](https://docs.rs#477)//! }
[478](https://docs.rs#478)//!
[479](https://docs.rs#479)//!
[480](https://docs.rs#480)//! let sink = MyMetricSink;
[481](https://docs.rs#481)//! let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", sink);
[482](https://docs.rs#482)//!
[483](https://docs.rs#483)//! client.count("my.counter.thing", 42);
[484](https://docs.rs#484)//! client.time("my.method.time", 25);
[485](https://docs.rs#485)//! client.count("some.other.counter", 1);
[486](https://docs.rs#486)//! ```
[487](https://docs.rs#487)//!
[488](https://docs.rs#488)//! ### Custom UDP Socket
[489](https://docs.rs#489)//!
[490](https://docs.rs#490)//! Most users of the Cadence `StatsdClient` will be using it to send metrics
[491](https://docs.rs#491)//! over a UDP socket. If you need to customize the socket, for example you
[492](https://docs.rs#492)//! want to use the socket in blocking mode but set a write timeout, you can
[493](https://docs.rs#493)//! do that as demonstrated below.
[494](https://docs.rs#494)//!
[495](https://docs.rs#495)//! ```rust,no_run
[496](https://docs.rs#496)//! use std::net::UdpSocket;
[497](https://docs.rs#497)//! use std::time::Duration;
[498](https://docs.rs#498)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[499](https://docs.rs#499)//! use cadence::{StatsdClient, UdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
[500](https://docs.rs#500)//!
[501](https://docs.rs#501)//! let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
[502](https://docs.rs#502)//! socket.set_write_timeout(Some(Duration::from_millis(1))).unwrap();
[503](https://docs.rs#503)//!
[504](https://docs.rs#504)//! let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
[505](https://docs.rs#505)//! let sink = UdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
[506](https://docs.rs#506)//! let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", sink);
[507](https://docs.rs#507)//!
[508](https://docs.rs#508)//! client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
[509](https://docs.rs#509)//! client.time("my.service.call", 214);
[510](https://docs.rs#510)//! client.count("some.event", 33);
[511](https://docs.rs#511)//! client.set("users.uniques", 42);
[512](https://docs.rs#512)//! ```
[513](https://docs.rs#513)//!
[514](https://docs.rs#514)//! ### Unix Sockets
[515](https://docs.rs#515)//!
[516](https://docs.rs#516)//! Cadence also supports using Unix datagram sockets with the `UnixMetricSink`  or
[517](https://docs.rs#517)//! `BufferedUnixMetricSink`. Unix sockets can be used for sending metrics to a server
[518](https://docs.rs#518)//! or agent running on the same machine (physical machine, VM, containers in a pod)
[519](https://docs.rs#519)//! as your application. Unix sockets are somewhat similar to UDP sockets with a few
[520](https://docs.rs#520)//! important differences:
[521](https://docs.rs#521)//!
[522](https://docs.rs#522)//! * Sending metrics on a socket that doesn't exist or is not being listened to will
[523](https://docs.rs#523)//!   result in an error.
[524](https://docs.rs#524)//! * Metrics sent on a connected socket are guaranteed to be delievered (i.e. they are
[525](https://docs.rs#525)//!   reliable as opposed to UDP sockets). However, it's still possible that the metrics
[526](https://docs.rs#526)//!   won't be read by the server due to a variety of environment and server specific
[527](https://docs.rs#527)//!   reasons.
[528](https://docs.rs#528)//!
[529](https://docs.rs#529)//! An example of using the sinks is given below.
[530](https://docs.rs#530)//!
[531](https://docs.rs#531)//! ```rust,no_run
[532](https://docs.rs#532)//! use std::os::unix::net::UnixDatagram;
[533](https://docs.rs#533)//! use cadence::prelude::*;
[534](https://docs.rs#534)//! use cadence::{StatsdClient, BufferedUnixMetricSink};
[535](https://docs.rs#535)//!
[536](https://docs.rs#536)//! let socket = UnixDatagram::unbound().unwrap();
[537](https://docs.rs#537)//! socket.set_nonblocking(true).unwrap();
[538](https://docs.rs#538)//! let sink = BufferedUnixMetricSink::from("/run/statsd.sock", socket);
[539](https://docs.rs#539)//! let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("my.prefix", sink);
[540](https://docs.rs#540)//!
[541](https://docs.rs#541)//! client.count("my.counter.thing", 29);
[542](https://docs.rs#542)//! client.time("my.service.call", 214);
[543](https://docs.rs#543)//! client.count("some.event", 33);
[544](https://docs.rs#544)//! client.set("users.uniques", 42);
[545](https://docs.rs#545)//! ```
[546](https://docs.rs#546)//!
[547](https://docs.rs#547)//! NOTE: This feature is only available on Unix platforms (Linux, BSD, MacOS).
[548](https://docs.rs#548)//!

# BufferedUdpMetricSink in cadence - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cadence/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/cadence/struct.BufferedUdpMetricSink.html

`pub struct BufferedUdpMetricSink { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Implementation of a `MetricSink` that buffers metrics before
sending them to a UDP socket.

Metrics are line buffered, meaning that a trailing “\n” is added after each metric written to this sink. When the buffer is sufficiently full and a write is attempted, the contents of the buffer are flushed to a UDP socket and then the metric is written to the buffer. The buffer is also flushed when this sink is destroyed.

The default size of the buffer is 512 bytes. This is the “safest”
size for a UDP packet according to the Etsy Statsd docs. The
buffer size can be customized using the `with_capacity` method
to create the sink if desired.

If a metric larger than the buffer is emitted, it will be written directly to the underlying UDP socket, bypassing the buffer.

Note that since metrics are buffered until a certain size is reached, it’s
possible that they may sit in the buffer for a while for applications
that do not emit metrics frequently or at a high volume. For these low-
throughput use cases, it may make more sense to use the `UdpMetricSink`
since it sends metrics immediately with no buffering.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cadence/sinks/udp.rs.html#489-494)

#### pub fn [from](https://docs.rs#method.from)<A>(sink_addr: A, socket: [UdpSocket](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/net/udp/struct.UdpSocket.html)) -> [MetricResult](https://docs.rs/type.MetricResult.html)<Self>

Construct a new `BufferedUdpMetricSink` instance with a default
buffer size of 512 bytes.

The address should be the address of the remote metric server to emit metrics to over UDP. The socket should already be bound to a local address with any desired configuration applied (blocking vs non-blocking, timeouts, etc.).

Writes to this sink are automatically suffixed with a Unix newline (‘\n’) by the sink and stored in a 512 byte buffer until the buffer is full or this sink is destroyed, at which point the buffer will be flushed.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use std::net::UdpSocket;
use cadence::{BufferedUdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
let sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::from(host, socket);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#failures)Failures

This method may fail if:

- It is unable to resolve the hostname of the metric server.
- The host address is otherwise unable to be parsed

```

21    let sock = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
22    let buffered = BufferedUdpMetricSink::from(("localhost", DEFAULT_PORT), sock).unwrap();

#### pub fn [with_capacity](https://docs.rs#method.with_capacity)<A>(
    to_addr: A,
    socket: [UdpSocket](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/net/udp/struct.UdpSocket.html),
    cap: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [MetricResult](https://docs.rs/type.MetricResult.html)<Self>

Construct a new `BufferedUdpMetricSink` instance with a custom
buffer size.

The address should be the address of the remote metric server to emit metrics to over UDP. The socket should already be bound to a local address with any desired configuration applied (blocking vs non-blocking, timeouts, etc.).

Writes to this sink are automatically suffixed with a Unix newline (‘\n’) by the sink and stored in a buffer until the buffer is full or this sink is destroyed, at which point the buffer will be flushed.

For guidance on sizing your buffer see the
[Statsd docs](https://github.com/etsy/statsd/blob/master/docs/metric_types.md#multi-metric-packets).

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use std::net::UdpSocket;
use cadence::{BufferedUdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
let sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::with_capacity(host, socket, 1432);
```

# BufferedUdpMetricSinkBuilder in cadence - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cadence/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/cadence/struct.BufferedUdpMetricSinkBuilder.html

`pub struct BufferedUdpMetricSinkBuilder { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Implementation of a builder pattern for `BufferedUdpMetricSink`.

The builder can be used to set the capacity of the buffer, how
often the hostname to send metrics to is re-resolved via DNS, and
how to handle errors when re-resolving the hostname. If these
options are *not* set, the default behavior is to only resolve
the hostname for sending metrics upon creation of the sink and
use a default buffer size, the same as when the sink is created
using `BufferedUdpMetricSink::from()`.

When the option to re-resolve hostnames to send metrics to is
enabled, a new thread is spawned when the sink is created that
will run until the sink is dropped, updating the `SocketAddr`
used for sending metrics in the background.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use std::net::UdpSocket;
use std::time::Duration;
use cadence::{BufferedUdpMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
let sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::builder()
    .with_capacity(1024)
    .with_resolver_period(Duration::from_secs(5))
    .with_resolver_error_handler(|e| {
        eprintln!("failed to re-resolve address: {}", e);
    })
    .build(host, socket)
    .unwrap();
```

Construct a new `BufferedUdpMetricSink` instance that emits metrics
using the provided address and socket.

The `BufferedUdpMetricSink` may optionally re-resolve the provided
address using DNS periodically. If provided, an error handler
will be invoked when the address cannot be resolved. The
error handler runs in the same thread as the resolver logic,
different from the thread the sink runs in, and must not
panic.

- It is unable to resolve the hostname of the metric server.

# BufferedUnixMetricSink in cadence - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cadence/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/cadence/struct.BufferedUnixMetricSink.html

`pub struct BufferedUnixMetricSink { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Implementation of a `MetricSink` that buffers metrics before
sending them to a Unix socket.

Metrics are line buffered, meaning that a trailing “\n” is added after each metric written to this sink. When the buffer is sufficiently full and a write is attempted, the contents of the buffer are flushed to a Unix socket and then the metric is written to the buffer. The buffer is also flushed when this sink is destroyed.

The default size of the buffer is 512 bytes. This is to be consistent with
the default for the `BufferedUdpMetricSink`. The buffer size can be customized
using the `with_capacity` method to create the sink if desired.

If a metric larger than the buffer is emitted, it will be written directly to the underlying Unix socket, bypassing the buffer.

Note that since metrics are buffered until a certain size is reached, it’s
possible that they may sit in the buffer for a while for applications
that do not emit metrics frequently or at a high volume. For these low-
throughput use cases, it may make more sense to use the `UnixMetricSink`
since it sends metrics immediately with no buffering.

Also note that unlike the UDP sinks, if there is no receiving socket at the path specified or nothing listening at the path, an error will be returned when metrics are emitted (though this may not happen on every write due to buffering).

# MetricBuilder in cadence - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cadence/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/cadence/struct.MetricBuilder.html

`pub struct MetricBuilder<'m, 'c, T>{ /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Builder for adding tags to in-progress metrics.

This builder adds tags, key-value pairs or just values, to a metric that
was previously constructed by a call to a method on `StatsdClient`. The
tags are added to metrics and sent via the client when `MetricBuilder::send()`
or `MetricBuilder::try_send()`is invoked. Any errors encountered constructing,
validating, or sending the metrics will be propagated and returned when those
methods are finally invoked.

Currently, only Datadog style tags are supported. For more information on the
exact format used, see the
[Datadog docs](https://docs.datadoghq.com/developers/dogstatsd/#datagram-format).

Adding tags to a metric via this builder will typically result in one or more extra heap allocations.

NOTE: The only way to instantiate an instance of this builder is via methods in
in the `StatsdClient` client.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#try_send)`.try_send()`

An example of how the metric builder is used with a `StatsdClient` instance
is given below.

```
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, NopMetricSink, Metric};
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("some.prefix", NopMetricSink);
let res = client.count_with_tags("some.key", 1)
   .with_tag("host", "app11.example.com")
   .with_tag("segment", "23")
   .with_tag_value("beta")
   .try_send();
assert_eq!(
    concat!(
        "some.prefix.some.key:1|c|#",
        "host:app11.example.com,",
        "segment:23,",
        "beta"
    ),
    res.unwrap().as_metric_str()
);
```
In this example, two key-value tags and one value tag are added to the metric before it is finally sent to the Statsd server.

[§](https://docs.rs#send)`.send()`

An example of how the metric builder is used with a `StatsdClient` instance
when using the “quiet” method is given below.

```
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, NopMetricSink, Metric};
let client = StatsdClient::builder("some.prefix", NopMetricSink)
    .with_error_handler(|e| eprintln!("metric error: {}", e))
    .build();
client.count_with_tags("some.key", 1)
   .with_tag("host", "app11.example.com")
   .with_tag("segment", "23")
   .with_tag_value("beta")
   .send();
```
Note that nothing is returned from the `.send()` method. Any errors encountered
in this case will be passed to the error handler we registered.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

### impl<'m, 'c, T> [MetricBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.MetricBuilder.html)<'m, 'c, T>

Add a key-value tag to this metric.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, NopMetricSink, Metric};
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("some.prefix", NopMetricSink);
let res = client.count_with_tags("some.key", 1)
   .with_tag("user", "authenticated")
   .try_send();

   "some.prefix.some.key:1|c|#user:authenticated",
   res.unwrap().as_metric_str()
);
```
```
17fn main() {
18    fn my_error_handler(err: MetricError) {
19        eprintln!("Error sending metrics: {}", err);
20    }
21
22    let client = StatsdClient::builder("my.prefix", NopMetricSink)
23        .with_error_handler(my_error_handler)
24        .build();
25
26    // In this case we are sending a distribution metric with two tag key-value
27    // pairs. If sending the metric fails, our error handler set above will
28    // be invoked to do something with the metric error.
29    client
30        .distribution_with_tags("latency.milliseconds", vec![10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
31        .with_tag("app", "search")
32        .with_tag("region", "us-west-2")
33        .send();
34
35    // In this case we are sending the same distribution metrics with two tags.
36    // The results of sending the metric (or failing to send it) are returned
37    // to the caller to do something with.
38    let res = client
39        .distribution_with_tags("latency.milliseconds", vec![10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
40        .with_tag("app", "search")
41        .with_tag("region", "us-west-2")
42        .try_send();
43
44    println!("Result of metric send: {:?}", res);
45}
```

16fn main() {
17    fn my_error_handler(err: MetricError) {
18        eprintln!("Error sending metrics: {}", err);
19    }
20
21    // Create a client with an error handler and default "region" tag

23        .with_error_handler(my_error_handler)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cadence/builder.rs.html#529-535)#### pub fn [with_sampling_rate](https://docs.rs#method.with_sampling_rate)(self, rate: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cadence/builder.rs.html#529-535)

#### pub fn [with_sampling_rate](https://docs.rs#method.with_sampling_rate)(self, rate: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self

Add a sampling rate to this metric.

The sampling rate is a float between 0 and 1 that determines the rate at which the metric is sampled. For example, a sampling rate of 0.5 would mean that the metric is sent 50% of the time. The sampling has to be done by the caller, cadence will simply forward it to the backend.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, NopMetricSink, Metric};
let client = StatsdClient::from_sink("some.prefix", NopMetricSink);
let res = client.distribution_with_tags("some.key", 1)
 .with_sampling_rate(0.5)
 .try_send();
assert_eq!(
 "some.prefix.some.key:1|d|@0.5",
 res.unwrap().as_metric_str()
);
```
```

#### pub fn [try_send](https://docs.rs#method.try_send)(self) -> [MetricResult](https://docs.rs/type.MetricResult.html)<T>

Send a metric using the client that created this builder.

Note that the builder is consumed by this method and thus `.try_send()`
can only be called a single time per builder.

);

37    // to the caller to do something with.
38    let res = client
39        .distribution_with_tags("latency.milliseconds", vec![10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
40        .with_tag("app", "search")
41        .with_tag("region", "us-west-2")
42        .try_send();
43
44    println!("Result of metric send: {:?}", res);
45}
```
```
19fn main() {
20    fn my_error_handler(err: MetricError) {
21        eprintln!("Error sending metrics: {}", err);
22    }
23
24    // Create a client with an error handler and default "region" tag
25    let client = StatsdClient::builder("my.prefix", NopMetricSink)
26        .with_error_handler(my_error_handler)
27        .with_tag("region", "us-west-2")
28        .build();
29
30    // In this case we are sending a counter metric with two tag key-value
31    // pairs. If sending the metric fails, our error handler set above will
32    // be invoked to do something with the metric error.
33    client
34        .count_with_tags("requests.handled", 1)
35        .with_tag("app", "search")
36        .with_tag("user", "1234")
37        .send();
38
39    // In this case we are sending the same counter metrics with two tags.
40    // The results of sending the metric (or failing to send it) are returned
41    // to the caller to do something with.
42    let res = client

46        .try_send();

```
Send a metric using the client that created this builder, discarding successful results and invoking a custom handler for error results.

By default, if no handler is given, a “no-op” handler is used that
simply discards all errors. If this isn’t desired, a custom handler
should be supplied when creating a new `StatsdClient` instance.

Note that the builder is consumed by this method and thus `.send()`
can only be called a single time per builder.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-5)Example

```
use cadence::prelude::*;
use cadence::{StatsdClient, MetricError, NopMetricSink};
fn my_handler(err: MetricError) {
    println!("Metric error: {}", err);
}
let client = StatsdClient::builder("some.prefix", NopMetricSink)
    .with_error_handler(my_handler)
    .build();
client.gauge_with_tags("some.key", 7)
   .with_tag("region", "us-west-1")
   .send();
```
```
16fn main() {
17    fn my_error_handler(err: MetricError) {
18        eprintln!("Error sending metrics: {}", err);
19    }
20

29    // handler set above will be invoked to do something with the metric error.

38    // id, meaning that the client's container id will be used.

# QueuingMetricSink in cadence - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cadence/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/cadence/struct.QueuingMetricSink.html

`pub struct QueuingMetricSink { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Implementation of a `MetricSink` that wraps another implementation
and uses it to emit metrics asynchronously, in another thread.

Metrics submitted to this sink are queued and sent to the wrapped sink
that is running in a separate thread. The wrapped implementation can
be any thread (`Sync` + `Send`) and panic (`RefUnwindSafe`) safe
`MetricSink`. Results from the wrapped implementation will be discarded.

The thread used for network operations (actually sending the metrics
using the wrapped sink) is created and started when the `QueuingMetricSink`
is created. The dequeuing of metrics is stopped and the thread stopped
when `QueuingMetricSink` instance is destroyed (when `.drop()` is
called).

This sink may be created with either a bounded or unbounded queue connecting the sink to the thread performing network operations. When an unbounded queue is used, entries submitted to the sink will always be accepted and queued until they can be drained by the network operation thread. This means that if the network thread cannot drain entries off the queue for some reason, it will grow without bound. Alternatively, if created with a bounded queue, entries submitted to the sink will not be accepted if the queue is full. This means that the network thread must be able to keep up with the rate of entries submit to the queue or writes to this sink will begin to fail.

Entries already queued are guaranteed to be sent to the wrapped sink
before the queuing sink is stopped. Meaning, the following code ends up
calling `wrapped.emit(metric)` on every metric submitted to the queuing
sink.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use cadence::{MetricSink, QueuingMetricSink, NopMetricSink};
let wrapped = NopMetricSink;
{
    let queuing = QueuingMetricSink::from(wrapped);
    queuing.emit("foo.counter:4|c");
    queuing.emit("bar.counter:5|c");
    queuing.emit("baz.gauge:6|g");
}
```
At the end of this code block, all metrics are guaranteed to be sent to the underlying wrapped metric sink before the thread used by the queuing sink is stopped.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Construct a new `QueuingMetricSink` instance wrapping another sink
implementation with an unbounded queue connecting them.

The `.emit()` method of the wrapped sink will be executed in a
different thread after being passed to it via a queue. The wrapped
sink should be thread safe (`Send + Sync`) and panic safe
(`RefUnwindSafe`).

The thread in which the wrapped sink runs is created when the
`QueuingMetricSink` is created and stopped when the queuing sink
is destroyed.

The queuing sink communicates with the wrapped sink by an unbounded queue. If entries cannot be drained from the queue for some reason, it will grow without bound.

[§](https://docs.rs#buffered-udp-sink-example)Buffered UDP Sink Example

In this example we wrap a buffered UDP sink to execute it in a different thread.

```
use std::net::UdpSocket;
use cadence::{BufferedUdpMetricSink, QueuingMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
let udp_sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
let queuing_sink = QueuingMetricSink::from(udp_sink);
```
```

#### pub fn [with_capacity](https://docs.rs#method.with_capacity)<T>(sink: T, capacity: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> Self

Construct a new `QueuingMetricSink` instance wrapping another sink
implementation with a queue of the given size connecting them.

The `.emit()` method of the wrapped sink will be executed in a
different thread after being passed to it via a queue. The wrapped
sink should be thread safe (`Send + Sync`) and panic safe
(`RefUnwindSafe`).

The thread in which the wrapped sink runs is created when the
`QueuingMetricSink` is created and stopped when the queuing sink
is destroyed.

The queuing sink communicates with the wrapped sink by a bounded queue of the provided size. When the queue is full, writes to this sink will fail until the queue is drained.

[§](https://docs.rs#buffered-udp-sink-example-1)Buffered UDP Sink Example

In this example we wrap a buffered UDP sink to execute it in a different thread.

```
use std::net::UdpSocket;
use cadence::{BufferedUdpMetricSink, QueuingMetricSink, DEFAULT_PORT};
let socket = UdpSocket::bind("0.0.0.0:0").unwrap();
let host = ("metrics.example.com", DEFAULT_PORT);
let udp_sink = BufferedUdpMetricSink::from(host, socket).unwrap();
let queuing_sink = QueuingMetricSink::with_capacity(udp_sink, 512 * 1024);
```
Return the number of times the wrapped sink or underlying worker thread
has panicked and needed to be restarted. In typical use this should always
be `0` but may be `> 0` for buggy `MetricSink` implementations.

Return the number of currently queued metrics. Note that due to the way this number is computed (submitted metrics - processed metrics), it is necessarily approximate.

# QueuingMetricSinkBuilder in cadence - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cadence/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/cadence/struct.QueuingMetricSinkBuilder.html

`pub struct QueuingMetricSinkBuilder { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Implementation of a builder pattern for `QueuingMetricSink`.

The builder can be used to set an error handler for the sink being
wrapped by a `QueuingMetricSink` as well as setting the capacity of
the `QueuingMetricSink`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use cadence::{MetricSink, QueuingMetricSinkBuilder, NopMetricSink};
let queue_size = 64 * 1024;
let wrapped = NopMetricSink;
let queuing = QueuingMetricSinkBuilder::new()
    .with_capacity(queue_size)
    .with_error_handler(|e| {
        eprintln!("Error while sending metrics: {:?}", e);
    })
    .build(wrapped);
queuing.emit("foo.counter:4|c");
```
